description: Solo team from Universiti Teknologi Malaysia (Johor Bahru). We built BanjirScope, which maps floods through monsoon cloud using NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar: before/after change detection on calibrated GCOV data, a 12-day flood timeline, and a free, open web map. Built for Malaysia's monsoon season.
summary: Monsoon floods happen under thick cloud, when optical satellites see nothing. BanjirScope uses NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar, which sees through cloud and night, to map where flooding happened. It compares a dry-date and a flood-date radar image from the same orbit, detects newly dark (flooded) ground with log-ratio change detection and automatic Otsu thresholds, and shows the result in an interactive web map with a before/after swipe, a 12-day timeline and the flooded area in km². On calibrated NISAR GCOV data it mapped about 1,334 km² of new flood water at the peak of the September 2026 Chao Phraya floods in Thailand, and it is ready to run on Malaysian floods as soon as new passes reach NASA's archive.
details: Live app: https://n7wl.github.io/banjirscope/ | Code: https://github.com/N7wl/banjirscope. What it does: BanjirScope turns NISAR radar passes over the same place into a flood map. Calm water reflects the radar pulse away from the satellite, so it looks dark; comparing a dry baseline (13 Aug 2026) with flood-date passes on the same orbit track and frame reveals ground that became newly dark. How it works: (1) find repeat-pass pairs in NASA's ASF archive with asf_search; (2) stream only the area of interest from each 6.6 GB NISAR L2 GCOV HDF5 file over HTTPS; (3) multilook to 30 m and apply a Lee speckle filter; (4) compute a log-ratio change image and pick water and change thresholds automatically with Otsu's method; (5) clean the mask and export web overlays and statistics. An extra layer flags flooded trees and towns, which get brighter at L-band (double bounce). A static Leaflet web app (GitHub Pages, no backend) offers a before/after swipe, a timeline of passes, layer toggles and flooded-area stats. Results: Chao Phraya floods, central Thailand (track 4, frame 81, HH): 484 km2 newly flooded on 18 Sep, about 1,334 km2 at the 30 Sep peak (1,200-1,330 km2 across reasonable thresholds), then 1,153 and 1,028 km2 as the water receded. Impact: radar works during floods, under cloud; the data is free, the code is open and event-agnostic, so agencies in Malaysia and the region could run it every 12 days. Malaysian events (Selangor/Perak, Nov 2026) are next. Tools: Python, asf_search, h5py, fsspec, NumPy/SciPy, scikit-image, OpenCV, pyproj, Leaflet; 22 automated tests with GitHub Actions CI. AI use: code, and the demo were built with help from an AI coding assistant (Claude); all maps and numbers are computed from NASA data, as stated in the README.
